title: Private VPC Deep Dive - Networking & Performance
summary: Deep technical session focused on Private VPC deployment networking for Redwood Private. Covered PrivateLink endpoints vs. NAT egress, subnet design, DNS and route table considerations, MTU and TCP/TLS tuning, and runtime performance impacts (KV cache, batching, quantization). Agreed next steps: share network diagram, run inside-VPC benchmark, provide security/KMS docs, and schedule follow-up with infra+security for pilot onboarding.
action_items: Mina Lopez (Redwood SE): produce suggested private-vpc network diagram and route table examples by 2026-04-20
Jordan Patel (Redwood AE): send pricing/commit options and Dedicated vs Private comparison by 2026-04-17
Grace Chen (ArborHealth): share existing VPC CIDR, subnet layout, and current NAT/GW config by 2026-04-18
Tom Wallace (ArborHealth Security): confirm KMS/HSM requirements and provide SOC2/ISO questions by 2026-04-22
next_steps: Run Redwood perf benchmark inside ArborHealth dev VPC (SE + customer infra) - target week of 2026-04-27
Redwood to share PrivateLink setup doc + CloudFormation template link
Schedule follow-up: 60-min pilot kickoff with infra & security on 2026-04-29
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): okay, welcome everyone, thanks for making time. we'll run through the private vpc network considerations and how that maps to runtime perf - feel free to stop me.
[00:12] Samir (ArborHealth): thanks, yeah we're excited — we've got two main goals: latency under 120ms p50 for short prompts and predictable throughput for batch scoring, and of course security constraints.
[00:25] Mina (Redwood SE): quick intros: Mina, I'm the SE working on Private deployments and perf. Jordan is your AE. we'll lean into KV cache, batching, and how network patterns like PrivateLink vs NAT affect tail latency.
[00:38] Grace (Network): hi, Grace — I'm our network engineer. we have a hub-and-spoke VPC, with centralized NAT gateway in the hub, some subnets private/ public per AZ. want to understand if PrivateLink is required or if NAT egress to the hosted control plane is okay.
[00:52] Mina: good question. high level: PrivateLink keeps control-plane traffic on AWS network path via VPC endpoints — minimizes hops and avoids public egress. NAT egress introduces an extra hop and potential SNAT scaling bottlenecks, which can add to tail latency and connection churn at high concurrency.
[01:08] Tom (Security): we need full audit logs, KMS key control, and no internet-facing control-plane traffic for our pilot. is PrivateLink mandatory to meet that?
[01:18] Jordan: not strictly mandatory but strongly recommended for strict security posture. PrivateLink + endpoint policies + endpoint network interfaces in your subnets gives you private connectivity. also supports VPC endpoints for SSM/Secrets Manager if you prefer to keep all control-plane calls internal.
[01:33] Lena (ML Infra): from the model side, our worry is KV cache misses across AZs. does Redwood's runtime keep KV caches warm per-GPU/host, and how does a multi-AZ placement affect latency for first tokens?
[01:45] Mina: good one — runtime keeps per-instance KV cache. for inference hot-paths we rely on sticky routing so repeated requests for same user/session hit same serving pool and benefit from cache. across AZs, cache miss will be higher if sticky routing isn't possible; network-induced variance (cross-AZ RTT) can add 2-8ms typical, but cache misses cause generation to fetch model weights or recompute attention states which is orders more.
[02:05] Jordan: we typically recommend co-locating clients that need the lowest latency in the same AZ as the serving pool; for multi-AZ redundancy we use smart routing: prefer local AZ, fallback to cross-AZ if needed. this balances SLOs and availability.
[02:20] Grace: ok, how does PrivateLink interact with cross-AZ traffic? endpoints exist in subnets in each AZ, right? so you'd create interface endpoints in each AZ you plan to route from.
[02:32] Mina: correct. you create an interface endpoint per AZ subnet — that keeps traffic local to AZ when possible. if you only create endpoint in one AZ, cross-AZ will happen and you pay inter-AZ charges and see higher latency.
[02:45] Samir: what about NAT throughput limits — we currently have a single NAT gateway in hub, can that throttle our connections at scale?
[02:54] Jordan: single NAT GW can be a bottleneck at very high ephemeral connection rates. for long-lived TLS connections or HTTP/2 multiplexing it's fine, but if your traffic pattern opens many short-lived connections per request (e.g., small clients, many ephemeral containers) you'll hit SNAT ephemeral port exhaustion or throughput ceilings. for high QPS we advise either PrivateLink or scaling NAT (multiple NAT gateways per AZ + route table per subnet) or using egress-only with proxy.
[03:19] Grace: worth noting we do autoscaling of NAT in hub, but not per-AZ. we can change.
[03:25] Mina: also keep MTU and path MTU in mind. our gRPC/TLS payloads can get a bit bigger with model telemetry; if there's fragmentation that adds jitter to latency. recommend consistent MTU 1500 unless you have jumbo frames internally, then validate MSS.
[03:39] Lena: switching to runtime perf — can you give concrete numbers for tokens/sec and p50/p99 with and without KV cache and batching?
[03:47] Mina: sure — caveat: numbers depend on model size, sequence length, and hardware. for a 13B model on a V100-ish profile, single request exemplary: cold KV miss p50 ~ 180ms, warm cache with small batch (1-4) p50 ~ 40-60ms, with batching of 8-16 optimized throughput we can hit ~800-1200 tokens/sec aggregate per GPU. for MPT-style prompts it's different, but these are representative.
[04:18] Jordan: important to note batching increases throughput but can increase tail latency if you wait to fill batch. we provide adaptive batching where we have a max_wait_ms (e.g., 10ms) and refill signals — that keeps p50 low while getting batching benefits.
[04:32] Samir: our target is p50 <=120ms for short prompts, and sustained throughput for nightly batch scoring at 20k reqs/min. doable with Private deployment?
[04:44] Mina: yes. for low-latency we’d pin capacity in a Dedicated pool in your VPC — Dedicated gives reserved GPUs and sticky routing. for 20k reqs/min we’d size for concurrency and ensure sufficient batching window. we'll run a perf bench inside your VPC to generate exact sizing.
[04:59] Grace: about DNS — we use split-horizon and Route53 private hosted zones. will Redwood resolve service endpoints via AWS PrivateLink DNS names or should we override?
[05:10] Mina: PrivateLink provides private DNS options; when enabled, AWS creates private DNS names that resolve to endpoint ENIs. If you manage your own private hosted zones, you can either delegate or create aliases. one caveat: some clients cache DNS aggressively, so TTLs and DNS caching can affect failover times. we recommend low TTLs for endpoints during rollout.
[05:30] Tom: on auth and KMS — can we use our BYOK HSM, or do you require Redwood-managed keys?
[05:38] Jordan: Redwood Private supports customer-managed keys and KMS integrations. for on-prem or air-gapped, we can integrate with HSMs via standard KMIP or AWS CloudHSM for VPC deployments. we'll need to capture the exact requirements in the security questionnaire.
[05:51] Samir: how about egress costs and data residency? If we keep everything inside VPC via PrivateLink, do we still see data egress charges?
[05:58] Mina: PrivateLink traffic stays on AZs and doesn't traverse the public internet, but there are AZ endpoint and cross-AZ data processing charges from AWS. these are often lower than NAT egress public internet charges and reduce security exposure. we'll model cost in the benchmarking spreadsheet.
[06:12] Grace: can you walk through a recommended subnet and route table config?
[06:16] Mina: yes — typical pattern: in each AZ, have at least two subnets: one for customer clients (private) and one for ENIs used by VPC endpoints. Create interface endpoints for Redwood control-plane in each AZ's endpoint subnet. Route table for client subnet points to local ENIs via endpoint-specific routes; keep a default route to NAT in hub for public egress if needed. Avoid routing through peering that forces hairpinning. Also apply security groups on the endpoints to limit traffic to known client subnets and ports (TLS 443).
[06:47] Jordan: also include flow logs and VPC reachability analyzer during initial setup to verify traffic paths. we provide a template CloudFormation and terraform examples.
[06:56] Samir: about KV cache and batching — if we run multiple model variants, does caching share across variants?
[07:03] Mina: KV cache is model-specific and checkpoint-specific; different quantization or sharded variants won't share cache. that means rolling upgrades or variant fallback will cause warmup penalties. recommended to pin model version and stage rollouts with warm pools to reduce cold cache events.
[07:19] Lena: quantization — do you recommend quantize to 4-bit for production? any perf/quality tradeoffs we should worry about?
[07:27] Mina: quantization to 4-bit (AWQ/QLoRA style) yields big memory and throughput gains, often 2-3x throughput depending on kernel support, but can introduce some quality drift — especially on instruction-following or long-range coherence. we recommend a small eval set; Redwood Optimize can run regression detection against your prompt set to flag quality regressions.
[07:47] Jordan: operationally we offer quantization profiles — you can set route policies to use lower-quant models for cheap background tasks and higher-precision for critical paths.
[07:58] Grace: any recommendations on connection keepalive and HTTP2 vs HTTP1.1?
[08:03] Mina: use HTTP2 or gRPC where possible to benefit from connection multiplexing — that reduces new TLS handshakes and SNAT port usage. set appropriate keepalive and idle timeouts; for long-lived clients mark them to reuse connections. for Lambdas or ephemeral containers that spin up frequently, consider a small connection pool or sidecar to amortize connect cost.
[08:22] Samir: can we get some concrete bench numbers from a Redwood-hosted vs in-vpc run to see delta?
[08:28] Mina: yes, that's one of the next steps — we'll run the same perf harness in your dev VPC. typical delta we've seen: PrivateLink in-VPC reduces median by 5-15ms vs public egress; NAT egress can add 10-30ms depending on topology and SNAT health. cross-AZ adds 2-8ms as mentioned. quantization and batching changes dominate longer tails.
[08:47] Tom: regarding logging and audit, do you stream audit logs to our Kinesis/S3?
[08:52] Jordan: yes, Private supports forwarding logs to customer destinations (Kinesis/S3/CloudWatch) and we can sign logs and provide truncated transcript behavior if needed for PHI. we'll need to validate retention policy for compliance.
[09:05] Mina: small gotcha — when using PrivateLink with custom DNS, your TLS validation must still match hostnames. if you rewrite hostnames internally, ensure SANs and certs validate or use SNI.
[09:18] Grace: good note. also curious about the behaviour under failover — if an AZ loses the endpoint, how fast can traffic reroute?
[09:26] Mina: DNS TTL and client failover strategies matter here. with endpoints in multiple AZs and low TTL + client re-resolve or using smart routing at load balancer level, failover can be seconds to tens of seconds. for ultra-low RTO we'd recommend a multi-AZ deployment with warm standby capacity and route preference changes at route tables.
[09:45] Samir: any suggestions for initial pilot sizing for our target p50 120ms and 20k reqs/min batch?
[09:52] Mina: propose pilot with 4 GPUs reserved in your VPC (profile matched to 13B optimized kernels), dedicated serving pool, and adaptive batching with max_wait 10ms. that should get you to target with headroom; we'll run a bench to confirm.
[10:07] Jordan: we'll attach a spreadsheet with sample cost math and perf numbers — you'll see tradeoffs between Dedicated reserved capacity and burstable hosted.
[10:16] Mina: also note that load tests should include realistic user patterns: small chat messages (20-50 tokens) and longer scoring jobs (200-1k tokens) to observe batching behavior.
[10:27] Grace: question on security groups — do endpoints require specific inbound rules?
[10:31] Mina: interface endpoints get ENIs and you control SGs. allow inbound from your client subnets on TLS port and restrict outbound to Redwood managed prefixes if you like. we also recommend least-privilege IAM policies on endpoints.
[10:43] Tom: follow up on compliance — can we get SOC2 attestation docs and penetration test reports?
[10:49] Jordan: yes, we'll share the SOC2 report and background pen-test summary; for more detailed material we have an NDA/SSLA path.
[10:58] Samir: ok let’s summarize next steps.
[11:00] Jordan: recap: Redwood to share network diagram and CF/Terraform templates, run perf bench in dev VPC with Mina + Grace + Lena, send security pack (SOC2, KMS whitepaper), and AE sends pricing and pilot contract options. customer to share VPC CIDR and current NAT config. set pilot kickoff 2026-04-29.
[11:18] Mina: I'll add action items in the follow-up email and attach the benchmark harness link and terraform example.
[11:24] Tom: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[11:27] Jordan: thanks — we'll follow up with notes and the templates.
[11:31] (call ends)
notes: Shared artifacts: link to 'Private VPC Networking Guide' (redwood.com/docs/private-vpc), perf benchmark harness (private link), pilot terraform template (s3://redwood-templates/private-vpc.tf)
Security: customer requested SOC2 report and KMS/HSM integration spec; Redwood to provide via secure link
